Checkstyle is the source of truth — when in doubt, run it.
- Collections take a plural name (`Collection<Point> points`)
- Long scope, long name; short scope, short name
- 4 spaces, never tabs; wrapped lines indent 8
- K&R braces — `{` on the same line
- Braces always, even for a single-statement `if` or loop
- One statement and one variable declaration per line
- Break after commas, before operators; assignment operators stay at EOL
- Member order: static fields, instance fields, constructors, methods
each group. No wildcard imports, no unused imports.
- Required on every public class and on public methods over one line long
(getters, setters and `main` are exempt; `*Test.java` is suppressed)
**Text hygiene** (enforced by `.github/check-*.sh`, so CI fails on these)
- No trailing whitespace — error in code, warning in `.md`
- LF line endings only, never CRLF

These are graded, not merely suggested.
- Avoid long methods — roughly 30 lines is the ceiling
- Avoid deep nesting and arrowhead code
- Avoid complicated expressions; compute intermediate values with names
- Avoid magic numbers — use named constants
- Make the code obvious; structure it logically
- Do not trip up the reader (unused parameters, inconsistent naming)
- SLAP hard — one level of abstraction per method
- Make the happy path prominent; use guard clauses
**Name well** — nouns for things, verbs for actions; standard words; names
that explain; neither too long nor too short; nothing misleading.
**Avoid unsafe shortcuts** — always use the default branch in a `switch`;
don't recycle variables; never leave an empty `catch` (checkstyle rejects it);
delete dead code rather than commenting it out; minimise variable scope;
**Comment minimally, but sufficiently** — don't repeat the obvious, write for
the reader, and explain WHAT and WHY, not HOW.
## Prevent functionality bugs and feature flaws
when designing, implementing and reviewing user-facing behaviour. Correctness
includes usability and matching reasonable user expectations, not merely
accepting values that fit a convenient data type.
**Design from the user's point of view**
- Before coding, define the normal use cases, plausible user mistakes and
harmful inputs. Deliberate sabotage need not be supported, but a likely
mistake must not crash the app, corrupt data or leave it unusable.
- Prefer the simplest useful feature, but do not omit behaviour essential for
the app to be reasonably useful. If a clearly better user experience needs
little extra effort, implement it rather than declaring it out of scope.
- Keep implementation, tests and the User Guide aligned. A mismatch is still
a bug regardless of whether the code or documentation is wrong.
- Do not impose arbitrary length, numeric or character restrictions merely to
simplify parsing or validation. Any limit must be justified by the product
domain and broad enough for realistic values.
- Accept symbols and formats that legitimate real-world values need. In
particular, command delimiters must not make common names or other expected
values impossible to enter; improve parsing where practical.
- Prefer warning to rejection for unusual but harmless values, such as a past
date or a richly annotated phone number. Block input only when accepting it
would hinder the software, make the data ambiguous or risk harm.
- Handle boundary values and arithmetic overflow where they can arise from a
plausible mistake. Very long values must not break the layout or hide so much
content that the feature becomes unusable.
- Error messages must identify the specific offending field/value and explain
the actual reason. Distinguish malformed input from a well-formed but invalid
value when practical; otherwise use an accurate combined message.
- Keep commands quick to type and easy to remember. Avoid needless case
sensitivity, long mandatory keywords and awkward special characters; where
useful, support both a short alias and a descriptive form.
- Match case sensitivity to the real-world concept. Names and search terms are
- Make search useful when users remember only part of the target. Consider
whether OR semantics, partial matching or other forgiving behaviour better
serves the documented use case than exact or AND-only matching.
- Keep terminal output presentable and non-alarming even though the GUI is the
primary interface; do not print misleading errors or stack traces during
- Do not rely only on exact string equality when case or insignificant
whitespace can differ. Normalize values consistently and test likely
- Prefer warning the user about a possible duplicate and letting them decide
when identity is ambiguous. State the detector's limitations clearly; never
imply that all duplicates are found when they are not.
- Retain at least AB3's support for human-editable data files: correctly edited
files must load, malformed edits may be rejected with clear diagnostics, and
the format must remain reasonably editable by hand.
- Do not silently discard or corrupt existing data after schema, parser or
validation changes. Add compatibility and malformed-data tests whenever a
- For every new or changed feature, add tests for the happy path, plausible
typing mistakes, empty and whitespace variants, case variants, realistic
symbols, boundary lengths/numbers, duplicate-like values and malformed
- Verify not only the returned result but also the exact user-facing error,
state after failure, persistence outcome and absence of unintended mutation.
- Review restrictions and defaults explicitly: each one needs a user-centered
rationale and must be documented if users can observe it.
Every issue carries a `type.*` label. Bugs also carry a `severity.*` label,
and anything scheduled carries a `priority.*` label and a milestone.
| `type.Epic` | A big feature that breaks down into smaller stories, e.g. search |
| `type.Enhancement` | An enhancement to an existing story |
| `type.Task` | Something to be done that is not a story, bug or epic, e.g. moving test code into a new folder |
| `severity.VeryLow` | Purely cosmetic, does not affect usage: typos, spacing, layout, colour, font. Cosmetic problems *only* |
| `severity.Low` | Unlikely to affect normal operation. Appears only in rare situations and causes minor inconvenience |
| `severity.Medium` | Causes occasional inconvenience to some users, but they can keep using the product |
| `severity.High` | Affects most users and causes major problems. Reserve this for flaws that make the product almost unusable for most users |

Most real bugs land in Low or Medium.

**TAB** is a desktop application tailored for teaching assistants (TAs) to manage student
contacts, tutorial rosters, and follow-up tasks. Optimized for users who prefer using Command
Line Interface (CLI) for inputs while retaining the visual clarity of a Graphical User
Interface (GUI), TAB lets fast typists navigate and update records faster than traditional
TAB is built for university teaching assistants—such as those at the NUS School of
Computing—who manage 150 to 250 students across multiple tutorial or lab slots each semester.
* **CLI-first speed:** Perform common tasks—adding students, tagging groups, and searching
records—entirely from the keyboard without reaching for a mouse.
* **Flexible tagging:** Group and filter students by module, tutorial group, lab slot,
or team to focus on the class at hand.
* **Follow-up tracking:** Flag students who require a reply or assistance, and filter
the list to see who still needs follow-up.
* **Offline and privacy-preserving:** Store student data locally in a plain-text JSON
file, ensuring sensitive student records remain off third-party cloud services.

This project uses Gradle for **build automation and dependency management**. **We recommend reading [this Gradle tutorial from se-edu/guides](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/gradle.html).**
The following commands perform common Gradle tasks.
* **`clean`**: Deletes the files created during the previous build tasks (e.g. files in the `build` folder).
* **`shadowJar`**: Uses the Shadow plugin to create the fat JAR file `build/libs/tab.jar`.
**`runShadow`**: Builds the application as a fat JAR, then runs it.
* **`checkstyleMain`**: Runs the code style check for the main code base.
**`checkstyleTest`**: Runs the code style check for the test code base.
* `./gradlew clean test`: Cleans the project before running all tests
This project uses GitHub Actions for CI. The necessary workflow configuration files are in `.github/workflows`. No further setup is required.
As part of CI, Gradle generates JaCoCo coverage reports from the tests, and CI uploads the coverage data to Codecov. Codecov then provides information about test coverage.

However, because Codecov is known to run into intermittent problems (e.g., report upload fails) due to issues on the Codecov service side, the CI is configured to pass even if the Codecov task failed. Therefore, developers are advised to check the code coverage levels periodically and take corrective actions if the coverage level falls below desired levels.
To enable Codecov for forks of this project, follow the steps given in [this se-edu guide](https://se-education.org/guides/tutorials/codecov.html).

In addition to Gradle checks, CI runs repository-wide checks. Unlike Gradle checks, which cover files used in the build, these checks cover every repository file and enforce rules that are hard to apply on development machines, such as line-ending requirements.

These checks are implemented as POSIX shell scripts, and thus can only be run on POSIX-compliant operating systems such as macOS and Linux. To run all checks locally on these operating systems, execute the following in the repository root directory:
Any warnings or errors will be printed out to the console.

* Checks are implemented as executable `check-*` scripts within the `.github` directory. The `run-checks.sh` script will automatically pick up and run files named as such. That is, you can add more such files if you need and the CI will do the rest.
* Check scripts should print out errors in the format `SEVERITY:FILENAME:LINE: MESSAGE`
* SEVERITY is either ERROR or WARN.
* FILENAME is the path to the file relative to the current directory.
* LINE is the line of the file where the error occurred and MESSAGE is the message explaining the error.
* Check scripts must exit with a non-zero exit code if any errors occur.

The ***Architecture Diagram*** given above explains the high-level design of TAB.
The following provides a quick overview of the main components and their interactions.

**`Main`** (consisting of classes [`Main`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T16-1/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/tab/Main.java) and [`MainApp`](https://github.com/AY2627S1-CS2103T-T16-1/tp/blob/master/src/main/java/seedu/tab/MainApp.java)) is in charge of TAB's launch and shut down.
* At TAB's launch, it initializes the other components in the correct sequence, and connects them up with each other.
* At shut down, it shuts down the other components and invokes cleanup methods where necessary.
The bulk of TAB's work is done by the following four components:
* [**`Model`**](#model-component): Holds the data of TAB in memory.
* [**`Storage`**](#storage-component): Reads data from, and writes data to, the hard disk.
[**`Commons`**](#common-classes) represents a collection of classes used by multiple other components.

This section describes some noteworthy details on how certain features are implemented.
`JsonStudentBookStorage` retains a separate copy of the student book loaded or
successfully saved at each path. Before saving, it rereads the current records
and compares them with that snapshot. A difference, a removed file, or an
unreadable replacement refuses the save; `LogicManager` then restores records
and the active filter. The snapshot advances only after a successful save.
Comparison uses parsed student records, so harmless JSON formatting changes do
not create a conflict. Each normal application startup reads the file before
issuing commands; callers saving without a prior read adopt the on-disk book
The comparison and replacement share an operating-system lock on
`.tab.json.lock` beside the real destination. Resolving symbolic links makes
windows reaching the same destination share a lock. A busy lock refuses the
save with retry guidance. The sidecar remains after closing TAB: deleting it
could allow different processes to lock different files with the same name.
Closing its channel releases the lock, including on a failed save or process
exit. This prevents stale TAB windows from overwriting each other's records;
it does not add concurrent multi-user editing. External editors do not honor
this lock and must be used with all TAB windows closed.
### Rolling back model changes when saving fails
`LogicManager` takes a copy of the student book and its active display filter
before executing a command. It compares the resulting student book with that
copy and writes to storage only when student records changed. Commands such as
`list`, `find`, `help`, and `exit` can therefore run even when the data file is
When a write fails, `LogicManager` restores both the student-book copy and the
previous filter before reporting the storage error. Restoring the filter as
well as the records matters because `add` normally resets the display to show
every student. The failed command consequently has no visible or
in-memory effect, and retrying it cannot apply the same change twice. A
confirmed `clear` follows the same save-and-restore path; its pending
confirmation is still removed before the save attempt so that a failure does
not leave a stale reply active.

the process's working directory. An exploded build keeps the working directory

`add` and `edit` mark their fields with options,
`add NAME -p PHONE [-e EMAIL] [--id NUS_STUDENT_ID] [-t TAG]... [--follow-up]` and
`edit INDEX [-n NAME] [-p PHONE] [-e EMAIL] [--id NUS_STUDENT_ID] [-t TAG]... [--follow-up | --no-follow-up]`,
where AB3 marked them with prefixes such as `p/`. The `edit` target may also
be an NUS Student ID that starts with a letter instead of a displayed index;
IDs starting with a digit must be addressed by index. The `--id` option sets
the ID field rather than selecting the target.
The value options have descriptive long aliases: `--name`, `--phone`,
`add` takes its name in the preamble. `edit` accepts `-n`/`--name` to change a
name, and `find` accepts the same option to search names.
A prefix has to be a sequence a value never contains, and no such sequence
exists for a name. `s/o`, `d/o`, `a/l` and `a/p` are ordinary parts of
Singaporean and Malaysian names, and `a/l` was in fact unreadable for as long
as an address field was marked `a/`. Widening the prefixes would only move the
collision somewhere else. Options move the problem out of the value entirely:
an option is a whole token, so a name is read as a name however it is spelled.
Parsing runs in two passes, the way a shell does it.
`CommandTokenizer` splits the arguments on whitespace and lets double quotes
group a value containing whitespace. A token records whether a quote took part in it,
because that is the only thing separating the value `-Ahmad` from the option
`-e`. A backslash escapes a quote or another backslash, so a value may hold
either; a backslash before anything else stays in the value, so nothing the User
typed disappears without being asked for.
An option appearing where a value is expected is read as the option before it
having been left empty, rather than as a value. `add John -p 123 -t -e` reports
that `-t` needs a value instead of storing `-e` as a tag. A value that really
does open with a hyphen is given in quotes.
`FlagTokenizer` reads the tokens. Those before the first option are the
*preamble*, joined with single ASCII spaces, which each command reads as
whatever it takes in that position: the name for `add`, so a name of several
words needs no quotes unless it would otherwise be misread, and the index for
`edit`. Each command names its own, in `AddCommand.FIELD_NAME` and
`EditCommand.FIELD_INDEX`, rather than the shared `CliFlags` doing it for
them. Each short and long marker resolves to the same `Flag`, so mixed aliases
for a single-valued field are duplicates rather than independent fields.
Value-taking options take the token after them, and `-t` or `--tag` repeats
for `add` and `edit`. The `tag` command takes exactly one tag through `-a`/`--add`
They also accept a value joined to any short or long marker by an equals sign.
`FlagTokenizer` splits only on the first equals sign, so later ones remain in
the value. An attached value is unambiguously part of its option when it opens
with a hyphen. An empty attached value must be quoted as in `--tag=""`, so an
accidental `--tag=` cannot clear data. `CommandTokenizer` records whether a
token began with a quote so a fully quoted `"--tag=T1"` remains a value, while
the quote around the value in `--tag="Lab 3"` does not hide the option marker.
For `edit`, tag values use `StringUtil.normalizeFieldValue` before validation.
A single normalized blank value clears all tags, including when the input holds
Unicode spaces. A blank beside other tag values is rejected with an explanation
that clearing requires the blank to be given on its own. Nonblank values are
still validated so every problem can be reported without silently discarding tags.
`--no-follow-up` option (alias `-nf`) instead record an empty value and consume
no following token. `add` accepts only `--follow-up`; `edit` accepts both to set
or clear the status, and `find` accepts both to filter by that status. This lets
absent option from a present marker without a separate representation. An
attached value on a presence-only option is refused specifically. An unknown
option names its marker without echoing an attached value, while a value-taking
option left without a value and a token belonging to no option are each
reported for what they are, rather than as one generic complaint.
`add` keeps its name before the options so names containing spaces need no
quotes. If the tokenizer refuses `-n` or `--name`, `AddCommandParser` adds a
placement hint to the existing error. A missing name gets the same hint,
so users familiar with the name options in `edit` can recover immediately.

* **Student book**: The collection of student records managed by TAB.
* **Student record**: The information TAB stores about one student, such as their name, NUS Student ID, phone number, email
* **TAB**: Teaching Assistant's Book; the desktop student-management application described in this guide.
* **Tag**: A user-defined label attached to a student record for grouping or filtering students.
* **Tag alias**: A user-defined shorthand for a longer tag (such as a shortcut for a tutorial group tag), distinct
from a command or shell alias.
* **Whitespace**: The Unicode characters with the `White_Space` property, as matched by Java's `(?U)\s`: `U+0009` to
and `U+3000`. This set excludes the zero-width space (`U+200B`), byte order mark (`U+FEFF`), zero-width non-joiner
(`U+200C`) and zero-width joiner (`U+200D`). It governs `CommandTokenizer`, normalized field values, and
to separate the command word from its arguments.

* The output logging level can be controlled by changing the `LOG_LEVEL` constant in the `LogsCenter` class.

`LogicManager` writes the command as it was typed, and `StudentBookParser` writes
how it read at `FINE`. The following commands also log their effects:
* `add`, `delete` and `edit` at `INFO`, with how many records the book then holds.
* `clear` at `INFO`, with how many it emptied, once the confirmation is given.
* `find` at `FINE`, with how many matched, since it changes only what is on screen.
`tag`, `list`, `exit` and `help` have no separate effect entries.
An entry counts records and names the index the User saw rather than writing the
student out. The command text in the log already holds whatever the User typed,
and repeating a name or an address in the entries after it puts more of someone's
details in the file for nothing.

Text pasted into the command box keeps its word boundaries: every separator
TAB splits a command on becomes a space, from a tab to a line break to the
soft line break a slide carries. This lets you paste names or values from
spreadsheet cells, slides and documents without joining their words. Pasted
text remains one command; inspect it before pressing Enter.
* Words in `UPPER_CASE` are the parameters to be supplied by the user.
For example, in `add NAME`, replace `NAME` with a value such as `John Doe`.
* A command word may be typed in any case, so `list`, `List` and `LIST` all
list your students. Only the first word is read this way: the rest of the
command keeps the capitals you typed, so `Find -n Alex` still looks for `Alex`.
Option spellings are case-sensitive, so `-P` is not the `-p` option.
* Items in square brackets are optional.
For example, `NAME [-t TAG]` can be used as `John Doe -t friend` or as `John Doe`.
* A vertical bar `|` separates alternatives; choose at most one and do not type the bar.
For example, `[--follow-up | --no-follow-up]` allows either option or neither.
* Items followed by `...` can appear zero or more times.
For example, `[-t TAG]...` may be omitted, or written as `-t friend` or as
* Parameters can be in any order.
For example, if the command specifies `-p PHONE -e EMAIL`,
`-e EMAIL -p PHONE` is also acceptable. A parameter given before any
option, such as the name in `add`, keeps its place at the front.
* Commands use options such as `-p` for fields, except positional parameters
such as the leading name in `add` or the target in `edit`. Value options also
have descriptive long aliases such as `--phone`; the command-specific
sections list them. Separate a value from its option with a space, as in
`--phone 91234567`, or join it with an equals sign, as in
`--phone=91234567`; short options accept both forms too. Only the first
equals sign is a separator, so the rest belong to the value. A value holding
spaces goes in double quotes after an option or after its equals sign, as in
`--tag="Lab 3"`. Quote any value opening with a hyphen when using a space;
after an equals sign it is already unambiguous. An equals sign still needs a
value after it. Where `edit` allows an empty value, write the deliberate
* If a non-repeatable option is given twice, TAB names the repeated option
and asks you to give it only once. For example, repeating `-f` reports
`Options given more than once: -f. Give each listed option only once.`
This also covers mixed short and long spellings, such as `-f` and `--follow-up`.
* An `INDEX` refers to a positive position in the **displayed** student list.
If it exceeds that list, TAB quotes the index and reports the number of students
currently shown; `list` restores all students before you choose an index again.
Indices up to 2147483647 can be read; a larger positive integer gets a specific
upper-bound message instead of being described as non-positive.
* Commands that take no parameters (`help`, `list`, `exit`, and `clear`)
reject unexpected input and report it without executing the command.
For example, `help 123` reports `help takes no arguments. Unexpected input:
"123".` Whitespace after the command is accepted, but quoted values,
* Invisible format characters are ignored wherever they appear, so a command
word or an index copied from a web page with a direction mark or a zero-width
space still runs as the command it looks like. The joiners some scripts need
for shaping are the exception and are kept.

* If you are using a PDF version of this document, be careful when copying and pasting commands that span multiple lines as space characters surrounding line-breaks may be omitted when copied over to the application.
TAB uses an English interface. Counts, displayed indices and data-file line
numbers use digits 0–9 regardless of your computer’s regional settings.

* anything else is in ordinary text

A word that opens a command is read as that command being typed: `del` and
`dele` reach `delete`, `cle` reaches `clear`, and `e` reaches both `edit` and
`exit`. Every command the word opens is named, because TAB cannot tell which
Any other word is matched letter by letter, and reaches a command when at most
two letters have to be added, removed, swapped or replaced to turn it into
that command, so `ls` reaches `list` and `dlte` reaches `delete`. A word that
is two letters out has to start with the same letter as the command, since the
first letter is the one you are least likely to get wrong. A word that is one
letter out may differ in it, so `felete` still reaches `delete`.
The comparison ignores case, so `Delte 3` is answered in the same way. A word
that reaches nothing, such as `dlt`, is answered with the pointer to `help`.
A word spelt correctly is no mistyping whatever case it is in: `List` and
`LIST` run `list` rather than being suggested back to you.
**Caution:** TAB never runs the command it suggests. Nothing is added, changed
or deleted by a mistyped command word, and what you typed stays in the command
box, so you can correct the word rather than type the command again.

Finds students matching every supplied search term within its selected field.
Provide at least one field term or one follow-up status option. Every search term needs a field option, which takes one word or one double-quoted phrase.
* Matching is case-insensitive and allows partial values: `find -n jas` matches `Jason`.
* All terms use **AND** matching, within and between fields. There is no OR search mode.
For example, `find -n Jason -t Lab -n Tan` requires both name terms and the tag term.
The order of the options does not matter.
* Field options restrict each term to that field. `find -t friend` excludes students
who have `friend` only in their name or email. Absent optional fields do not match.
* Repeat an option to require more terms. `find -n Jason -t lab -t tutorial` matches
Jason Lim with tag `lab tutorial` and Jason Zhou with tags `lab 5` and `tutorial 3`,
but excludes Jason Tan with only tag `lab`. Terms may match the same tag or different tags.
* Enclose a multi-word term in double quotes: `find -n "Jason Tan"` requires that whole
phrase in the name. `find -t "lab tutorial"` requires the phrase within one tag;
separate tags are never joined. Repeated spaces inside a phrase are collapsed to one space.
* Name searches ignore Latin accents and straight/curly apostrophe differences:
`find -n nguyen` matches `Nguyễn Văn An`, `find -n jose` matches `José Rivera`,
and `find -n O'Brien` matches `Sean O’Brien`. The stored spelling stays unchanged.
* Unicode case variants match in names and tags: `find -n σ` matches `ΝΙΚΟΣ`,
and `find -t οσ` matches tag `ΟΣ`, consistent with adding/removing that tag.
Accents and apostrophes remain significant in tags and other fields.
* Single quotation marks do not group words; use double quotes for phrases.
* Bare terms are refused, including a name given before any option. Use a field option
for every term. An extra word after an option is also refused; repeat the option or quote a phrase.
This replaces the earlier unqualified cross-field search syntax and OR matching.
* Status options take no value. `find -f` lists students needing follow-up, and `find -nf`
lists students not needing it. Combine a status option with field terms using AND:
`find -f -n Jason -t Lab` requires the status, name fragment and tag fragment.
Omitting both status options searches students of either status.
* Use at most one status option. Conflicting options (`-f` with `-nf`) or a repeated
status option, including mixed aliases, are refused without changing the results.
* To include a literal double quote or backslash inside a term, escape it with a backslash:
`\"` or `\\`. An unclosed quote or an empty or whitespace-only term is refused
without changing the current student list.
* Quote a term starting with a hyphen, or attach it with `=`:
`find -t "-Lab"` and `find --tag=-Lab` search for the literal tag text `-Lab`.
* Phone terms containing only digits, grouping spaces and phone punctuation (`+`, `-`, `(`, `)`, `.`)
also search the phone with all non-digit characters removed, provided the term contains a digit.
all match `+65 9123 4567` or `91234567`. `find -p +6591234567` also matches the number
stored with the country code. Quote terms containing spaces;
copied Unicode spaces work too. Equivalent Unicode decimal digits match across scripts:
Displayed and saved numbers keep their formatting. Terms containing other characters, such as `"ext 21"`,
and punctuation-only terms match the stored text.
* TAB reports the number of matches: `Found 0 students.`, `Found 1 student.` or `Found 3 students.`.
* `find -n john` returns students whose names contain `john`, including `John Doe`.
* `find -t "Lab 3"` returns students with a tag containing the phrase `Lab 3`.
* `find -n Alice -t "Lab 3"` requires both the name fragment and the tag phrase.
* `find -p 91234 -t friend` requires both the phone fragment and the tag fragment.
* `find --id a0123 -p 9123 -e nus.edu` requires all three field conditions.
Deletes the specified student from the student book.
Format: `delete INDEX` or `delete NUS_STUDENT_ID` or `delete --id NUS_STUDENT_ID`
* An `INDEX` deletes the student at that position in the displayed student list.
* An `NUS_STUDENT_ID` deletes the student who holds that ID, wherever they are in
the book — even while a search is hiding them. The match ignores case.
* `--id NUS_STUDENT_ID` names the value as an ID, which an ID starting with a digit
needs — the plain form would read it as an index. `-i` works in place of `--id`.
* If an out-of-range numeric target is also a stored NUS Student ID, TAB suggests
the exact `delete --id VALUE` command. Leading zeroes in an ID are preserved.
A bare number that is a valid displayed position still deletes by that position.
* The command result identifies the removed record (`Deleted student: NAME; Phone: PHONE...`)
so you can verify exactly which student was deleted from the book.
* `delete` takes no field values, so a value found after the target is refused with
`Unexpected value after INDEX: "..."`, naming the part to remove, as in
`Unexpected value after INDEX: "2". delete accepts one index and nothing else.`
* `list` followed by `delete 2` deletes the 2nd student in the student book.
* `find -n Betsy` followed by `delete 1` deletes the 1st student in the results of the `find` command.
* `delete A01234567X` deletes the student holding the NUS Student ID `A01234567X`.
* `delete a01234567x` deletes the same student, because matching an ID ignores case.
* `delete --id 1A2B3C` deletes the student whose NUS Student ID is `1A2B3C`, which the plain
form would otherwise read as an index.
* `find -n Alex` followed by `delete A02345678G` deletes Charlotte Oliveiro, whose NUS Student
ID is `A02345678G` in the sample data, even while the search hides her.

**Q**: How do I transfer my data to another computer?
**A**: Install TAB on the other computer, then copy `data/tab.json` from your
previous TAB home folder to the same place beside the new JAR, creating the
`data` folder if it is not there. A new install has no data file to overwrite:
TAB writes one only when a command changes a record, so a fresh TAB that has
only been looked at leaves the folder without it. Copy the file while TAB is
closed, since TAB rewrites it from its own copy at the next change.
